e00.title: The Lost Garden
e00.subtitle: A road closed, and a first promise
story: In the beginning God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and breathed the breath of life into the man he had shaped from the dust. Adam and Eve walked with him and enjoyed every fruit of the garden. Only from the tree in the middle of the garden, the tree that gives knowledge of good and evil, he told them not to eat. If they ate from it, he said, they would surely die.

But the serpent came to Eve and whispered: did God really say that? You will not die at all; your eyes will be opened and you will be like God. Eve picked the fruit and ate, and gave some to Adam, who was with her. In that moment they knew shame, and when they heard the sound of God walking in the evening breeze, they hid among the trees.

Adam, where are you? God called. That day sin came between people and God, and through sin death came into the world. God told the serpent that the woman’s offspring would crush its head. Then he made garments of skin and clothed them, sent them out to the east of the garden, and set cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. The story of how that closed road is opened again now begins with a young girl in Nazareth.

words.text: You may eat freely from any tree in the garden. But do not eat from the tree that gives knowledge of good and evil, for on the day you eat from it you will certainly die.
Where are you?
I will set hostility between you and the woman, between your offspring and hers. Her offspring will crush your head, and you will bite his heel.

e00.note: Genesis 3:15 has long been called the “first gospel”. The New Testament finds in Jesus Christ the answer to who the woman’s offspring is that crushes the serpent’s head. Paul called him “the last Adam”.
e00.reflect: Faced with his question, where are you, can I answer him instead of hiding?
e00.credit: Giovanni di Paolo, The Creation of the World and the Expulsion from Paradise, 1445 (detail) · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain

e01.title: The Annunciation
e01.subtitle: A story that began with a girl's yes
story: Nazareth, a hill village in Galilee. On an ordinary day in a small town whose name appears nowhere in the Old Testament, a light stood before Mary, a young girl promised in marriage to Joseph of the house of David. It was the angel Gabriel, sent from God.

“Rejoice, you who are so richly favored.” To the trembling girl the angel brings news almost too hard to believe. She will bear a child, his name will be Jesus, and he will be king of a kingdom without end. With a shaking voice, Mary accepts the word.

Joseph, her betrothed, meant to end the engagement quietly, but in a dream he heard the same news from an angel and took Mary as his wife. While the world knew nothing of it, heaven was beginning its greatest story in the lowest of places.

words.text: Do not be afraid, Mary. God has shown you his favor. Nothing is impossible for God.
I am the Lord's servant. Let it happen to me just as you have said.
Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. Name the son Jesus, for he will rescue his people from their sins.

e01.note: Nazareth is thought to have been a small farming village of only a few hundred people. It was so obscure that in John's Gospel Nathanael asks, 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?'
e01.reflect: Faced with a calling I cannot explain, could I answer yes the way Mary did?

quiz.q: What name did the angel give Mary for her child?
quiz.explain: 'Jesus' means 'the Lord saves' (Lk 1:31; Mt 1:21). 'Immanuel' is a title from the prophecy of Isaiah that Matthew quotes.

e01.credit: James Tissot, The Annunciation, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e02.title: Night in Bethlehem
e02.subtitle: A night with no room, a song over the fields
story: The Roman emperor Augustus ordered a census across the whole empire. Joseph left Nazareth with Mary, heavy with child, and walked the long road to Bethlehem, the town of his ancestor David. The unfamiliar town was already crowded with people.

There was no room for them to stay. That night Mary gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in cloth, and laid him in a manger, the trough where animals feed. In the cold air, only the baby's faint breath rose like mist.

In the fields nearby, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks through the night when suddenly the glory of the Lord blazed around them. The angel's news was followed by the praise of a heavenly army filling the night sky, and the shepherds hurried off and found the baby in the manger. Mary treasured all these things deep in her heart.

words.text: Do not be afraid. I bring you good news that will be great joy for all the people. Today in the town of David your Savior is born, Christ the Lord.
Glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth peace to the people in whom he delights.
Come, let us go to Bethlehem and see with our own eyes this thing the Lord has made known to us.

e02.note: The Greek word 'kataluma', usually rendered 'inn', can also mean the guest room of a family home. So some interpret Jesus as being born on the lower floor of a house where livestock were kept, or in a cave.
e02.reflect: If God chose the humblest of mangers, in what low place of my own life might I meet him?

quiz.q: What sign did the angel give the shepherds?
options: A star resting over a house
A prince born in a palace
A baby wrapped in cloth, lying in a manger
A lamb offered at the Temple
quiz.explain: The angel said the sign would be 'a baby wrapped in cloth and lying in a manger' (Lk 2:12). The star belongs to Matthew's account of the Magi.

e02.credit: James Tissot, The Adoration of the Shepherds, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e03.title: Simeon and Anna in the Temple
e03.subtitle: A light in the eyes of two who waited a lifetime
story: On the eighth day the child was circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel had said. When the days of purification were complete, Joseph and Mary carried him up to the Temple in Jerusalem and, as the Law required, offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.

Just then Simeon, a righteous and devout old man, was led by the Spirit into the Temple. He had lived with a promise that he would not die before he saw the Christ. He took the child in his arms and praised God, then told Mary that a day would come when sorrow would pierce her heart like a sword.

Anna, too, came near, the daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, a widow of eighty-four. She was a prophet who never left the Temple, fasting and praying night and day. She gave thanks to God and spoke about the child to everyone who was waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

words.text: Lord, now let your servant go in peace, as you promised. My eyes have seen your salvation.
This child will cause many to fall and many to rise. And your own heart will ache as if pierced by a sword.

e03.note: Leviticus 12 allows a family of limited means to offer two birds instead of a lamb. That Joseph and Mary offered birds shows that this was a poor family.
e03.reflect: Like Simeon and Anna, facing a promise that takes long to arrive, what keeps my hope alive?

quiz.q: From which tribe was the prophet Anna, who met the infant Jesus in the Temple?
quiz.explain: Anna was the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher (Lk 2:36).

e03.credit: James Tissot, The Aged Simeon, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e04.title: The Magi Follow the Star
e04.subtitle: Men from the far east who read the stars
story: In the days of King Herod, Magi from the east appeared in the streets of Jerusalem asking where the one born king of the Jews might be. They had seen his star rise, they said, and had come to worship him. Herod was shaken at their words, and all Jerusalem trembled with him.

Herod summoned the chief priests and the teachers of the Law and pressed them on where the Christ was to be born. The answer was Bethlehem, in the writing of the prophet Micah. The king called the Magi in secret, learned exactly when the star had appeared, and asked them to report back once they found the child, so that he too might worship him.

As they set out, the star they had seen in the east went ahead of them and stopped over the place where the child was. Overjoyed, the Magi entered the house, bowed down before the child at his mother's side, and offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Then, warned in a dream, they returned home by another road.

words.text: Where is the one born king of the Jews? We saw his star rising and have come to worship him.

words.who: The chief priests and teachers of the Law
words.text: Bethlehem in the land of Judah, you are by no means a small town. From you will come a leader who will shepherd my people Israel.
Go and search carefully for the child, and when you find him, report to me, so that I may go and worship him too.

e04.note: The 'magoi' were likely a class of scholars who studied the stars in Persia or Babylonia. Scripture does not say how many there were; the tradition of three comes from the three gifts.
e04.reflect: The Magi knelt with joy at the end of a long journey. What am I searching for on my own long road?

quiz.q: Which of these was NOT a gift the Magi gave the child Jesus?
quiz.explain: The Magi offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Mt 2:11). The thirty pieces of silver were the money Judas later received.

e04.credit: James Tissot, The Magi Journeying, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e05.title: Flight into Egypt
e05.subtitle: Escape by night, and weeping in Ramah
story: After the Magi had gone, the angel of the Lord appeared again to Joseph in a dream. Herod was searching for the child to kill him, so Joseph was to take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt. That very night Joseph rose and set out into the darkness.
Crossing the desert roads to the south, the family reached Egypt and stayed there until Herod died. Matthew records that this fulfilled the words of Hosea: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.'

When Herod realized the Magi had outwitted him, he flew into a rage. Reckoning from the time he had learned from them, he killed every boy two years old and under in Bethlehem and all its surroundings. In that wailing Matthew hears Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted.

words.text: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is searching for the child to destroy him.
A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and bitter mourning. Rachel weeps for her children and will not be comforted, because they are no more.

e05.note: Alexandria in Egypt had a large Jewish community at the time, making it a natural refuge. Bethlehem was a small town, so the children killed probably numbered a few dozen or fewer.
e05.reflect: When the violence of the world falls on the innocent, am I someone who stays beside their weeping?

quiz.q: Herod ordered the killing of boys in Bethlehem under what age?
quiz.explain: Based on the time he had learned from the Magi, Herod killed all the boys two years old and under (Mt 2:16).

e05.credit: James Tissot, The Flight into Egypt, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e06.title: Return to Nazareth
e06.subtitle: A child growing up in an unknown village
story: When Herod died, the angel came again to Joseph in a dream in Egypt. Those who sought the child's life were dead, so he was to return to the land of Israel. Joseph took the child and his mother and started for home.
But word came that Archelaus, Herod's son, was ruling Judea in his father's place. Afraid, Joseph was warned again in a dream, turned north toward Galilee, and settled in a town called Nazareth.

In that small village on the hill, the child grew. Luke notes briefly that he grew strong and was filled with wisdom, and that the grace of God rested on him. Quiet years passed, far from the eyes of the world.

words.text: Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel. Those who wanted the child dead are gone.
The child grew and became strong, full of wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.

e06.note: Herod the Great is thought to have died around 4 BC, after which Archelaus ruled Judea and Herod Antipas ruled Galilee. Archelaus ruled so harshly that Rome removed him in AD 6.
e06.reflect: In ordinary days that no one notices, how am I growing?

quiz.q: Joseph was afraid to go to Judea because of who was ruling there?
quiz.explain: Joseph was afraid when he heard that Archelaus, Herod's son, was ruling Judea in his father's place (Mt 2:22).

e06.credit: James Tissot, The Return from Egypt, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e07.title: Twelve, in His Father's House
e07.subtitle: The boy found after three days, in his Father's house
story: Every year at Passover, Joseph and Mary went up to Jerusalem. When Jesus was twelve, they made the pilgrimage as was the custom. On the way home after the festival, his parents walked a full day's journey, assuming their son was somewhere in the group.

They searched among relatives and friends, but the boy was nowhere to be found. Returning to Jerusalem, after three days they found him in the Temple. He was sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and everyone who heard him was amazed at his understanding and his answers.

To his anxious mother's question the boy answered calmly, but his parents did not understand what he meant. He went down with them to Nazareth and lived in obedience to them, growing in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and people. Mary kept all these things in her heart.

words.text: Why were you looking for me? Didn't you know I had to be in my Father's house?
Child, why have you done this to us? Your father and I have been searching for you in such distress.

e07.note: Galileans made the pilgrimage in large village caravans, so a child's absence could go unnoticed for a day. Nazareth to Jerusalem was a walk of three or four days.
e07.reflect: Where is the place I truly belong right now? Where is the Father's house in my heart?

quiz.q: After how many days did Joseph and Mary find Jesus in the Temple?
quiz.explain: After three days his parents found Jesus in the Temple, sitting among the teachers (Lk 2:46).

e07.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Found in the Temple, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e08.title: Baptism in the Jordan
e08.subtitle: Heaven opened above the river
story: Leaving Nazareth in Galilee, Jesus, now about thirty, came to the banks of the Jordan. Among the crowd lined up before John, who was calling for a baptism of repentance, John recognized him and tried to stop him, saying that he himself ought to be baptized by Jesus.
Jesus persuaded John that it was right to do this now. At last the waters of the Jordan covered him and streamed away. Luke tells us that as he came up from the water and was praying, heaven opened.

The Spirit of God came down on him like a dove, and a voice rang out from heaven: my beloved Son, in whom I delight. The carpenter of Nazareth, who had lived so quietly, now stepped out before the world.

words.text: Let it be this way for now. It is right for us to do this and so fulfill all that God's righteousness requires.
You are my Son, whom I love. In you I take great delight.

e08.note: John's Gospel calls the place where John was baptizing 'Bethany beyond the Jordan'. It is thought to be Al-Maghtas, on the Jordan east of Jericho. Luke gives Jesus' age at this time as about thirty.
e08.reflect: If the voice from heaven calls me a beloved child too, am I living today out of that identity?

quiz.q: When Jesus was baptized, the Spirit came down like what?
quiz.explain: The Spirit of God descended like a dove and rested on him (Mt 3:16; Mk 1:10; Lk 3:22).

e08.credit: James Tissot, The Baptism of Jesus, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e09.title: Forty Days in the Wilderness
e09.subtitle: Three temptations overcome in a starving body
story: Before the water of baptism had even dried, the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness. Mark notes that he was with the wild animals. After forty days and nights without food, when at last he felt hunger, the tempter came to him.

If you are the Son of God, the whisper went, turn these stones into bread. Then the tempter set him on the highest point of the Temple and told him to throw himself down, and on a high mountain he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, promising them all if he would bow down and worship.

Each time, Jesus answered with the words of Scripture. At last, at his firm command to be gone, the devil left, and angels came and served him. Luke adds that the devil departed for a time, waiting for another opportunity.

words.text: It is written: people do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.
Away with you, Satan! It is written: worship the Lord your God, and serve him alone.
It is also written: do not put the Lord your God to the test.

e09.note: The Judean wilderness is a dry stretch of limestone hills running from east of Jerusalem down to the Dead Sea. Matthew and Luke give the second and third temptations in a different order.
e09.reflect: Facing hunger, the longing to be recognized, and the lure of easy success, what word holds me steady?

quiz.q: In the first temptation, what did the devil tell Jesus to turn the stones into?
quiz.explain: The devil said that if he were the Son of God, he should command the stones to become bread (Mt 4:3; Lk 4:3).

e09.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Tempted in the Wilderness, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e10.title: Come and See: The First Disciples
e10.subtitle: An invitation at four in the afternoon
story: At Bethany beyond the Jordan, John was standing with two of his disciples when he saw Jesus passing by and cried out: look, the Lamb of God. At those words the two disciples followed him. Jesus turned and asked them what they were looking for.

When they asked where he was staying, he said, come and see. It was about four in the afternoon. One of the two who spent that day with him, Andrew, went to find his brother Simon and told him they had found the Messiah, and Jesus gave Simon a new name, Cephas.

The next day, on his way to Galilee, Jesus called Philip of Bethsaida. Philip ran to tell Nathanael. Nathanael scoffed that nothing good could come from Nazareth, but when Jesus said he had already seen him under the fig tree, his doubt gave way and he confessed his faith.

words.text: What are you looking for? Come and see.
You are Simon, son of John. From now on you will be called Cephas.
Before Philip called you, while you were under the fig tree, I saw you.
Teacher, you are the Son of God. You are the King of Israel!

e10.note: 'The tenth hour' counts from sunrise in the Jewish way, so it means about four in the afternoon. 'Cephas' is Aramaic for rock; in Greek it is 'Peter'.
e10.reflect: When someone invites me to come and see, can I take the first step before my doubts do?

quiz.q: What new name did Jesus give Simon, Andrew's brother?
quiz.explain: Jesus told Simon he would be called 'Cephas', which is translated 'Peter' (Jn 1:42).

e10.credit: James Tissot, The Calling of Saint John and Saint Andrew, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e11.title: The Wedding at Cana
e11.subtitle: The first sign, water turned to wine
story: A wedding feast was held in Cana of Galilee. The mother of Jesus was there, and Jesus and his disciples had been invited too. In the middle of the celebration, amid laughter and song, the wine ran out.

His mother came and told him they had no more wine. Even when he answered that his hour had not yet come, she told the servants to do whatever he said. Six large stone jars stood there, the kind used for Jewish purification rites.

The servants filled every jar to the brim with water and drew some out, and when the master of the feast tasted it, he called the bridegroom over. Everyone else serves the good wine first, he said, but you have saved the best until now. This was the first sign Jesus performed, and his disciples believed in him.

words.text: Fill the jars with water. Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.
Mother, what does that have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.
Whatever he tells you, do it.

e11.note: Wedding feasts then could last up to a week, and running out of wine was a great shame for the family. Each jar is thought to have held two or three metretes, roughly 80 to 120 liters.
e11.reflect: When something in my life runs dry, can I fill the jars with the faith that says, do whatever he tells you?

quiz.q: How many stone jars stood at the wedding feast in Cana?
quiz.explain: There were six stone jars used for purification rites (Jn 2:6).

e11.credit: James Tissot, The Marriage at Cana, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e12.title: Overturning the Temple Tables
e12.subtitle: His Father's house turned into a market
story: As Passover drew near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem. The Temple courts were packed with merchants selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and with money changers seated at their tables. The bellowing of animals and the clink of coins had crowded out the place of prayer.

He made a whip out of cords and drove out all the sheep and cattle, scattered the money changers' coins, and overturned their tables. To the dove sellers he said, do not turn my Father's house into a marketplace. His disciples remembered the psalm that says zeal for your house will consume me.

When asked what sign he would show, he answered: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. People scoffed that the Temple had taken forty-six years to build, but the temple he spoke of was his own body. Only after the resurrection did his disciples understand these words.

words.text: Get these out of here. Stop turning my Father's house into a place of trade.
Tear down this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.
This Temple took forty-six years to build, and you will raise it in three days?

e12.note: Herod began rebuilding the Temple around 20 BC. The money changers exchanged coins from many lands into Tyrian shekels for paying the Temple tax. John places this event early in Jesus' ministry.
e12.reflect: In the temple of my heart, what has crowded out the place of prayer?

quiz.q: How many years did the Jewish leaders say it had taken to build the Temple?
quiz.explain: They said, 'This Temple has been under construction for forty-six years' (Jn 2:20).

e12.credit: James Tissot, The Merchants Chased from the Temple, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e13.title: Nicodemus Comes by Night
e13.subtitle: The secret of the wind, heard in the dark
story: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, came to Jesus at night. In a room lit by a single flickering lamp, he spoke carefully. No one could perform the signs you do, he said, unless God were with him.

Jesus answered that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born anew. When Nicodemus asked how an old man could be born again, Jesus spoke of being born of water and the Spirit, of the work of the Spirit that is like the wind, no one knowing where it comes from or where it goes.

Then came the words that, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up. The confession that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, and the words that light had come into the world but people loved the darkness more, lingered long in the stillness of the night.

words.text: I tell you the truth: unless someone is born anew from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.
God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son, so that all who believe in him will not perish but have eternal life.
The wind blows where it wills. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with all who are born of the Spirit.

e13.note: The Greek word 'anothen', rendered 'anew', means both 'again' and 'from above'. Nicodemus appears again later at Jesus' burial, bringing myrrh and aloes.
e13.reflect: Am I still stuck in a faith that only dares to come to him carefully, under cover of night?

quiz.q: When Jesus said the Son of Man must be lifted up, he compared it to what Moses lifted up in the wilderness. What was it?
quiz.explain: He said that just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up (Jn 3:14; Num 21:9).

e13.credit: James Tissot, Interview between Jesus and Nicodemus, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e14.title: The Well at Sychar
e14.subtitle: Noon at the well, two thirsty people
story: Leaving Judea for Galilee, Jesus passed through Samaria and came to a town called Sychar, where Jacob's well was. Tired from the road, he sat down by the well. It was around noon, with the sun directly overhead. His disciples had gone into town to buy food.

When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, he asked her for a drink. The conversation began with her astonishment that a Jew would ask a Samaritan woman for water. It went on to living water that ends thirst forever, to her five husbands, and to the question of where God should be worshiped.

When the woman said the Messiah was coming, he told her, I am he, the one speaking to you. She left her water jar behind and ran into town to call the people. Many Samaritans came and urged him to stay, and he remained two days. This man, they declared, is truly the Savior of the world.

words.text: Whoever drinks this water will thirst again. Whoever drinks the water I give will never thirst; it becomes in them a spring welling up to eternal life.
God is spirit, so those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth.
My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to carry his work through to the end.
Come and see! There is a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?

e14.note: Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem, and there was deep hostility between them and the Jews. Jacob's well, which still survives near modern Nablus, is said to be about 40 meters deep.
e14.reflect: Have I ever been the first to speak to someone on the road that others avoid?

quiz.q: At the Samaritans' request, how long did Jesus stay in Sychar?
quiz.explain: When the Samaritans asked him to stay, Jesus remained there two days (Jn 4:40).

e14.credit: James Tissot, The Woman of Samaria at the Well, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e15.title: Life from Afar
e15.subtitle: A father who turned back trusting a single word
story: After two days in Samaria, Jesus returned to Galilee. The Galileans, who had seen what he did at the festival in Jerusalem, welcomed him. He came again to Cana, where he had turned water into wine.

A royal official who lived in Capernaum heard the news and hurried to him. His son was dying of a fever. Even when Jesus said that people would not believe unless they saw signs and wonders, the man begged him to come down before the child died. Jesus said only this: go, your son will live.

The man believed the word and set off. On his way down, his servants met him with the news that the boy was alive. When he asked when the boy had begun to recover, they answered that the fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour. It was the very hour he had heard the word. He and his whole household believed.

words.text: Go. Your son will live.
Unless you see signs and wonders, you will never believe.
Lord, please come down before my child dies.

e15.note: Cana to Capernaum is about 25 kilometers, a road that descends to the shore of the Sea of Galilee, below sea level. The seventh hour is about one in the afternoon, and John calls this the second sign Jesus performed in Galilee.
e15.reflect: When I must turn back holding nothing but a word, with no visible proof, can I walk that road?

quiz.q: According to the servants, when did the official's son's fever break?
quiz.explain: The servants said, 'The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour', the very hour when Jesus had said, 'Your son will live' (Jn 4:52–53).

e15.credit: James Tissot, The Healing of the Officer's Son, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e16.title: Rejected in Nazareth
e16.subtitle: Those closest to him were the first to turn away
story: A Sabbath morning in the synagogue of Nazareth, the hometown where he grew up. When Jesus stood up to read, as was his custom, he was handed the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He slowly unrolled it, found a passage, and read: good news for the poor, freedom for the captives.

He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down, and every eye in the synagogue was fixed on him. At his declaration that this word had been fulfilled today, the people marveled, yet soon began to wonder. Isn't this Joseph's son?

When Jesus spoke of how Elijah was sent to the widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon, and Elisha to Naaman the Syrian, the synagogue boiled with rage. They dragged him to the edge of the cliff on which their town was built. But he passed right through the middle of them and went on his way.

words.text: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. He has sent me to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, and sight to the blind.
This scripture you have just heard with your own ears is fulfilled here today.
I tell you the truth: no prophet is welcomed in his own hometown.

e16.note: Synagogue worship included readings from the Law and then the Prophets, and it was customary to sit down to teach after reading. That is why every eye was on Jesus when he returned the scroll and sat down.
e16.reflect: Because it feels so familiar, am I failing to recognize the grace that has come to stand right beside me?

quiz.q: Which prophet's scroll was Jesus handed to read in the synagogue at Nazareth?
quiz.explain: Luke records that the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Jesus (Lk 4:17). The passage he read was the opening of Isaiah 61.

e16.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Unrolls the Book in the Synagogue, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e17.title: Fishers of People
e17.subtitle: A single word dropped over empty nets
story: The shore of Gennesaret. Fishermen who had toiled all night for nothing had beached their boats and were washing their nets. As the crowd pressed in to hear the word, Jesus stepped into Simon's boat, asked him to push out a little from the land, and sat down to teach the people from the water.

When he had finished speaking, Jesus told them to go out into the deep water and let down the nets. Simon said they had caught nothing all night, yet he lowered the nets as he was told. At once so many fish filled them that the nets began to tear, and their partners' boat was called over until both boats were close to sinking.

Simon fell at Jesus' knees. Go away from me, he said, for I am a sinful man. But Jesus told him not to be afraid. Simon and Andrew, and James and John the sons of Zebedee, brought their boats to shore, left everything behind, and followed him.

words.text: Come, follow me. I will make you into people who fish for others.
Row out into the deep water, and let down your nets for a catch.
Do not be afraid. From now on you will be bringing in people.
Lord, go away from me. I am a sinful man.

e17.note: In 1986 a fishing boat about eight meters long was found in the mud on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Dated to around the time of Jesus, it gives a sense of the size of the boats fishermen used then.
e17.reflect: In the place where all my night's labor has left only empty nets, can I once more let them down at his word?

quiz.q: Who was the father of James and John, who were called while mending nets in their boat?
quiz.explain: James and John left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Jesus (Mk 1:19–20).

e17.credit: James Tissot, The Miraculous Draught of Fishes, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e18.title: A Long Day in Capernaum
e18.subtitle: From synagogue to doorstep, and prayer before dawn
story: The Sabbath, in the synagogue at Capernaum. Jesus taught nothing like the scribes. His words went straight to the heart, like the words of one with authority. Then a man gripped by an unclean spirit cried out: Jesus of Nazareth, I know who you are. You are the Holy One of God.

Jesus rebuked it, and the spirit shook the man and left him. Leaving the synagogue, they entered the home of Simon and Andrew, where Simon's mother-in-law lay sick with fever. Jesus took her by the hand and raised her up, the fever left her, and at once she rose and served them.

When the sun went down and the Sabbath ended, the whole town crowded at the door with their sick, and many were healed. The next morning, while it was still dark, Jesus prayed alone in a deserted place, and when the disciples found him, he told them they would go on to other towns.

words.text: Let us go on to the nearby towns. I must bring the message there too. This is what I came out to do.
Be silent, and come out of him.
Everyone is looking for you.

e18.note: The white limestone synagogue standing in Capernaum today was built in the fourth or fifth century. The black basalt foundation beneath it is thought to be the remains of the synagogue of Jesus' day.
e18.reflect: When a busy day is over, do I make time to stand alone before God in the stillness of early morning?

quiz.q: In the house they visited after leaving the synagogue, who was healed of a fever?
quiz.explain: Jesus took Simon's mother-in-law by the hand and raised her up, the fever left her, and she got up and served them (Mk 1:30–31; Lk 4:38–39).

e18.credit: James Tissot, The Healing of Peter's Mother-in-law, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e19.title: The Day the Roof Opened
e19.subtitle: The faith of friends opened the roof
story: Word spread that Jesus was back in Capernaum, and the house where he was staying filled in an instant. There was no room even at the door. Pharisees and teachers of the law from every corner of Galilee and Judea, and from Jerusalem, were sitting there among them.

Then four men came carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. Finding the way in blocked, they climbed onto the roof, scraped away the earth, and broke through. Through the falling sunlight and dust, the man was lowered on his mat right down in front of Jesus.

Seeing their faith, Jesus declared that the man's sins were forgiven. The scribes muttered to themselves that this was blasphemy. Then Jesus told him to get up and walk, and in front of everyone he picked up his mat and walked out. All of them praised God, saying they had never seen anything like this.

words.text: Child, your sins are forgiven.
So that you may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, I tell you: get up, take your mat, and go home.
Which is easier: to say your sins are forgiven, or to say get up, take your mat, and walk?

e19.note: Houses in Galilee usually had flat roofs of branches and clay laid over wooden beams, reached by an outside stair. Luke describes the man being let down through the tiles.
e19.reflect: For someone near me who cannot come on their own, am I willing to break through a roof if that is what it takes to bring them to Jesus?

quiz.q: How many men carried the paralyzed man and broke open the roof?
quiz.explain: Mark records that four men carried the paralyzed man (Mk 2:3). They dug through the roof, made an opening, and lowered him down (Mk 2:4).

e19.credit: James Tissot, The Palsied Man Let Down through the Roof, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e20.title: Matthew at the Tax Booth
e20.subtitle: A man who rose from a place of scorn
story: Jesus had gone out by the lake to teach the crowd, and as he walked along he came to the tax booth. Sitting there was Levi son of Alphaeus, also called Matthew, a tax collector scorned for siding with the powerful and collecting taxes from his own people.

Follow me. It was a single phrase. Levi got up, left everything behind, and followed him. Then he threw a great feast at his house, and many tax collectors and sinners reclined at the table with Jesus and his disciples.

The scribes of the Pharisees challenged the disciples. Why does your teacher eat and drink with people like these? Jesus heard and answered. The healthy do not need a doctor, the sick do. I came to call exactly such as these.

words.text: The healthy do not need a doctor, the sick do. I did not come to call those who think themselves righteous, but sinners.
Follow me.
Go and learn what this means: what I desire is mercy, not sacrifice.

e20.note: Capernaum lay on the road where the Galilee of Herod Antipas met the territory of Philip, so it likely had a toll booth. Tax collectors often took more than was owed and were treated like sinners.
e20.reflect: Whom do I avoid sharing a table with, and whom would Jesus invite to that seat?

quiz.q: What other name do Mark and Luke use for Matthew the tax collector?
quiz.explain: Matthew's Gospel calls him Matthew (Mt 9:9), while Mark and Luke call him Levi (Mk 2:14; Lk 5:27). Mark identifies him as the son of Alphaeus.

e20.credit: James Tissot, The Calling of Saint Matthew, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e21.title: The Pool of Bethesda
e21.subtitle: The day thirty-eight years of waiting ended
story: A Jewish festival, at the pool of Bethesda beside the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem. In the shade of five colonnades lay crowds of the blind, the lame, and the withered. Among them was a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years.

Jesus asked him, Do you want to be well? Instead of answering, the man poured out his complaint. There was no one to put him in the pool when the water was stirred, and while he was making his way, someone else always went in first. Jesus told him to get up, pick up his mat, and walk, and at once he was healed and walked.

That day was the Sabbath. The Jewish leaders objected to a mat being carried on the Sabbath and to a healing on the Sabbath. When Jesus answered that his Father was still working and so he was working too, they sought all the more to kill him, for he was making himself equal with God.

words.text: Do you want to be made well?
Get up. Pick up your mat and walk.
My Father is still at work even now, and so I am at work too.
Truly I tell you, whoever hears my word and trusts the one who sent me has eternal life, and has already crossed from death into life.

e21.note: Excavations near the Church of Saint Anne in the late nineteenth century uncovered two large reservoirs. Some suggest that colonnades around the four sides and along the wall between the pools would match the five porches John describes.
e21.reflect: Faced with a pain I have long grown used to, can I truly answer that I want to be healed?

quiz.q: How many years had the man Jesus healed at the pool of Bethesda been ill?
quiz.explain: John records that the man had been ill for thirty-eight years (Jn 5:5).

e21.credit: James Tissot, The Piscina Probatica or Pool of Bethesda, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e22.title: Appointing the Twelve
e22.subtitle: Names called after a night of prayer
story: In those days Jesus went up a mountain to pray. As the sun set, the stars came out, and dawn broke again, he prayed to God all night long. The hillside overlooking the Sea of Galilee was still, and in that stillness a weighty choice was ripening.

When day came, Jesus called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he named apostles. Mark sets down the purpose this way: that they might be with him, that he might send them out to proclaim the message, and that they might have authority to drive out demons.

Simon Peter and his brother Andrew. James and John, called the sons of thunder. Philip and Bartholomew, Matthew and Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who would later become the traitor. One by one, ordinary names were called.

words.text: Jesus went out to the mountain to pray and spent the whole night in prayer to God. When day came, he called his disciples and chose twelve of them.
Jesus called those he wanted, and they came to him. He appointed twelve to be with him and to be sent out to proclaim the message.

e22.note: The number twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel. Among the four lists of apostles in the New Testament, Thaddaeus and Judas son of James trade places, and many see them as two names for the same man.
e22.reflect: If the first reason Jesus called me is simply to be with him, am I staying by his side today?

quiz.q: What did Jesus do on the mountain the night before choosing the twelve apostles?
options: He prayed to God all night
quiz.explain: Luke records that Jesus went to the mountain and spent the whole night praying to God, and when day came he chose the twelve (Lk 6:12–13).

e22.credit: James Tissot, Ordaining of the Twelve Apostles, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e23.title: Teaching on the Mountain
e23.subtitle: A voice on the hillside that overturned the world's wisdom
story: A hillside overlooking the Sea of Galilee. Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain and sat down, and his disciples drew close. On a slope where the wind swept through the grass, a teaching began that turned the world's wisdom upside down. Blessed are the poor in spirit.

You are the salt and the light of the world. Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Pray to your Father who sees in secret. Look at the birds of the air and the lilies of the field. Do not worry about tomorrow, but seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

The teaching ended with a story of two houses. Whoever hears these words and does them is like a house built on rock, which does not fall when the rain pours and the wind beats against it. The crowds were amazed, for he taught them as one with authority, not like their scribes.

words.text: Blessed are those who know they have nothing within to lean on. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them.
Love your enemies, and pray for those who torment you. That is how you become children of your Father in heaven.
So do not worry ahead of time about tomorrow. Tomorrow will carry its own worries. Today's trouble is enough for today.
Whoever hears my words and lives by them is like a wise man who built his house on rock. Storms come, and that house still stands.

e23.note: Matthew presents this as a teaching given on a mountain, Luke as one given on a level place. The Church of the Beatitudes on a hill north of the Sea of Galilee was built in 1938, following a tradition that honored this spot as the site of the sermon.
e23.reflect: Of the words I have heard today, is there one I am actually putting into practice as the foundation of my life?

quiz.q: Jesus said that whoever hears his words and does them is like someone who built a house where?
quiz.explain: Whoever hears and does these words is like a wise man who built his house on rock, and it did not fall in the storm (Mt 7:24–25). Whoever hears but does not do them is like a house built on sand (Mt 7:26–27).

e23.credit: James Tissot, The Sermon of the Beatitudes, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e24.title: The Centurion's Faith
e24.subtitle: Only say the word
story: In Capernaum there was a centurion whose servant, dear to him, was sick and dying. Hearing about Jesus, the centurion sent some Jewish elders to ask for help. The elders pleaded earnestly. He loves our nation, they said, and he even built our synagogue for us.

As Jesus drew near the house, friends sent by the centurion delivered his words. Lord, do not trouble yourself. I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Only say the word. I too am a man who takes orders and gives them.

Jesus was amazed, and he turned to the crowd following him. Not even in Israel, he said, had he found such faith. When the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant already well. A single word had crossed the distance and reached a life.

words.text: I tell you, not even in Israel have I found faith as great as this.
Go. Let it be done for you just as you have believed.
Many will come from east and west and take their places at the feast of the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Lord, I am not one who deserves to have you in my house. Just say one word, and my servant will be healed.

e24.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. Galilee was then the territory of Herod Antipas, so this man was most likely a Gentile officer serving under Antipas.
e24.reflect: Without any visible proof, can I trust him completely and ask him only to say the word?

quiz.q: When the Jewish elders recommended the centurion, what did they say he had built for them?
quiz.explain: The elders said the centurion loved the Jewish nation and had built their synagogue for them (Lk 7:4–5).

e24.credit: James Tissot, The Centurion, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e25.title: The Funeral at Nain
e25.subtitle: A funeral procession halted at the town gate
story: Nain, a small village at the foot of a hill in southern Galilee. As Jesus approached the town gate with his disciples and a large crowd, a funeral procession was coming out. The dead man was the only son of a widow, and many townspeople walked beside her, weeping.

When the Lord saw the mother, his heart went out to her. Do not weep. Then he came forward and touched the bier, and those carrying it stood still. Before the gate, where the wailing had faded, the voice of Jesus rang out. Young man, I say to you, get up.

The dead young man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother. Fear seized them all, and they glorified God. A great prophet has risen among us. God has come to visit his people.

words.text: Do not weep.
Young man, I say to you, get up.
A great prophet has appeared among us. God has come to look after his people.

e25.note: Nain lay at the foot of the Hill of Moreh, and on the far side of that hill was Shunem, where Elisha raised the Shunammite woman's son. That memory may be part of why the people thought of a great prophet.
e25.reflect: Like Jesus, who came near though no one had asked him, do I draw near first to someone's grief?

quiz.q: What did Jesus touch before raising the young man?
quiz.explain: Jesus came forward and touched the bier, and those carrying it stood still (Lk 7:14).

e25.credit: James Tissot, The Resurrection of the Widow's Son at Nain, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e26.title: The Woman Who Wet His Feet with Tears
e26.subtitle: One who is forgiven much loves much
story: A Pharisee invited Jesus to a meal. The guests reclined around the table, leaning on one side with their feet stretched out behind them. Then a woman known in that town as a sinner came in carrying an alabaster jar of perfume and stood behind him at his feet.

The woman wept. As her tears fell on Jesus' feet, she wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet, and poured the perfume over them. Simon, the host, thought to himself: if this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman she is. Jesus began to tell him a story about two debtors.

Five hundred denarii and fifty denarii. If both were forgiven, which would love more? Turning toward the woman, Jesus asked Simon, Do you see this woman? Then he said to her, Your sins are forgiven. Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.

words.text: Her many sins have been forgiven, and that is why she has loved so greatly. One who is forgiven little loves little.
Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.
Do you see this woman? When I came into your house, you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and dried them with her hair.

e26.note: Luke does not give this woman's name. Mary Magdalene is introduced separately in the very next scene, so there is no basis for treating them as the same person. That identification came from an interpretation in the Western church in the late sixth century.
e26.reflect: Do I know how great a forgiveness I have received, and is that knowing becoming the measure of my love?

quiz.q: In the parable Jesus told Simon, what debts did the two people owe?
options: Five hundred denarii and fifty denarii
One hundred denarii and ten denarii
One thousand denarii and one hundred denarii
quiz.explain: One owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and the lender canceled both debts (Lk 7:41–42).

e26.credit: James Tissot, The Meal in the House of the Pharisee, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e27.title: Parables by the Sea
e27.subtitle: The kingdom of God in a tiny seed
story: That day Jesus left the house and sat down by the sea. Such a great crowd gathered that he got into a boat and sat on the water, while the people lined the shore. His voice carried out over the gentle waves. Listen. A sower went out to sow.

Seed that fell on the path was eaten by birds, seed on rocky ground quickly withered, and seed among thorns was choked. But seed that fell on good soil bore fruit, thirty, sixty, and a hundred times over. Jesus added: whoever has ears, let them hear.

The stories went on. The mustard seed, smallest of all planted in the ground. Yeast mixed into flour. Treasure hidden in a field, and a pearl of great price. A net that hauls in fish of every kind. The kingdom of God begins in what is small and hidden, and in the end it changes everything.

words.text: The seed sown on good soil stands for those who hear the word and welcome it, and they bear fruit thirty, sixty, and a hundred times over.
The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed. When planted it is smaller than any seed, but it grows larger than every plant, and birds nest in its shade.
The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. Whoever finds it goes off in joy, sells all he has, and buys that field.
Do you light a lamp only to cover it with a bowl or put it under a bed? Will you not set it on a lampstand?

e27.note: Between Capernaum and Tabgha lies a small inlet called the Bay of the Sower. Research suggests its sloping shore gathers sound like a natural amphitheater, so a voice from a boat could reach thousands.
e27.reflect: Is my heart right now more like the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, or the good soil?

quiz.q: Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to something a woman mixed into three measures of flour until all the dough rose. What was it?
quiz.explain: The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until all of it had risen (Mt 13:33).

e27.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Preaches in a Ship, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e28.title: Rebuking the Wind and the Sea
e28.subtitle: Who is this man?
story: As the day full of parables drew to a close, Jesus said, Let us cross to the other side. Leaving the crowd behind, the disciples took him along in the boat, and other boats set out with them. Then a furious squall arose, and the waves broke over into the boat.

The water was rising, yet Jesus was asleep in the stern with his head on a cushion. The disciples woke him. Teacher, do you not care that we are about to die? Even the voices of these fishermen, raised on the sea, were shaking with fear.

Jesus got up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, Quiet. Be still. The wind ceased, and the sea lay calm as a mirror. Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith? Filled with an even greater fear, the disciples asked one another, Who then is this?

words.text: Quiet. Be still.
Why are you so fearful? Do you still have no faith?
Let us cross over to the other side of the lake.
Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

e28.note: The Sea of Galilee lies in a basin about two hundred ten meters below sea level. When cool air from the surrounding highlands suddenly rushes down the valleys, a calm lake can be whipped into a violent storm in moments.
e28.reflect: When Jesus seems to be asleep in the storms of my life, which do I hold on to, fear or faith?

quiz.q: Where in the boat was Jesus sleeping when the storm arose?
options: On the nets in the bow
In the stern, on a cushion
quiz.explain: Mark records that Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the stern, at the back of the boat (Mk 4:38).

e28.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Stilling the Tempest, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e29.title: The Man Among the Tombs
e29.subtitle: A darkness stronger than chains, a word stronger still
story: Across the lake, in the country of the Gerasenes. As Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man who lived among the tombs came running. Not even iron chains could hold him. Night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he cried out and cut himself with stones.

He fell down before Jesus and shouted, Jesus, Son of the Most High God, do not torment me. When asked his name, he answered, Legion, for we are many. The unclean spirits entered a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rushed down the steep bank into the sea.

People came running and found him sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid, and begged Jesus to leave. When the man asked to go with him, Jesus told him to go home and tell what the Lord had done. And he spread the news all through the Decapolis.

words.text: Go home to your family. Tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.
Unclean spirit, come out of this man.
What is your name?

e29.note: Mark and Luke call it the region of the Gerasenes, Matthew the region of the Gadarenes, and the manuscripts disagree on the name. At Kursi on the eastern shore stand the remains of a fifth century Byzantine monastery commemorating this event.
e29.reflect: If Jesus sent me home, what would I tell those closest to me about what he has done for me?

quiz.q: About how many pigs were in the herd the unclean spirits entered?
quiz.explain: Mark records that the herd numbered about two thousand (Mk 5:13). In his account of the same event, Matthew mentions two possessed men (Mt 8:28).

e29.credit: James Tissot, My Name is Legion, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e30.title: Talitha Koum
e30.subtitle: Beyond the news that it was too late
story: When Jesus crossed the lake again, Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, came running and fell at his feet. My little daughter is dying. Come and lay your hands on her. As Jesus went with him, a great crowd surrounded him and pressed against him. In that crush was a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.

She had spent all she had on many doctors and only grown worse. Believing that if she touched just his cloak she would be healed, she reached out from behind. In that instant the bleeding stopped. Who touched my clothes? To the trembling woman who came forward, Jesus said, Daughter, your faith has made you well.

Just then people came from the synagogue leader's house. Your daughter is dead. Jesus said, Do not be afraid, only believe, and he went into the room with only Peter, James, John, and the child's parents. He took her by the hand and said, Talitha koum, and the twelve year old girl got up and walked.

words.text: Talitha koum. Little girl, I say to you, get up.
Do not be afraid. Only believe.
Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace. Be free of your suffering and be whole.
Why all this commotion and weeping? The child is not dead. She is asleep.

e30.note: Talitha koum is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke. Mark preserves a few of Jesus' Aramaic words just as they sounded, such as Ephphatha, Abba, and Eloi, and then explains their meaning.
e30.reflect: When the news comes that it is already too late, can I hold on to the words, do not be afraid, only believe?

quiz.q: What does Talitha koum, the words Jesus spoke to Jairus's daughter, mean?
quiz.explain: Talitha koum is Aramaic for little girl, get up (Mk 5:41). The girl was twelve years old (Mk 5:42).

e30.credit: James Tissot, The Daughter of Jairus, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e31.title: A Feast in the Wilderness
e31.subtitle: Five barley loaves and two fish
story: The disciples had come back from their mission worn out. They crossed by boat to a quiet place near Bethsaida to rest a while, but people had heard and hurried ahead along the shore. Jesus had compassion on them, for they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he taught them until the sun was low.

You give them something to eat. The disciples were at a loss. Philip reckoned that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough, and all Andrew could find was a boy's five barley loaves and two fish. It was spring, with Passover near, and the people sat down in groups on the green grass.

Jesus looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the bread, and shared it, and the food passed from hand to hand without end. Five thousand men ate their fill, and the leftover pieces filled twelve baskets. When the people tried to seize him and make him king, Jesus withdrew to the mountain alone.

words.text: You yourselves give them something to eat.
Come away by yourselves to a quiet place and rest a little while.
Gather up all the leftover pieces, so that nothing is wasted.

e31.note: It is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels. Luke names the place as Bethsaida, thought to be near the mouth of the Jordan on the northeast shore of the Sea of Galilee. John notes that the boy's loaves were barley bread, the food of the poor.
e31.reflect: Can I offer the Lord the small and humble things I hold in my hands?

quiz.q: After everyone had eaten, how many baskets of leftover pieces were there?
quiz.explain: When the leftover pieces were gathered, they filled twelve baskets (Mt 14:20; Mk 6:43; Lk 9:17; Jn 6:13). Seven baskets belongs to a different event, the feeding of the four thousand.

e31.credit: James Tissot, The Miracle of the Loaves and Fishes, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e32.title: The One Who Comes Over the Water
e32.when: AD 29, spring · the fourth watch of the night
e32.subtitle: On a windy night, he comes walking on the water
story: After sending the crowds away, Jesus had the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, and he went up the mountain alone to pray. As the night deepened, a headwind rose. For hours the disciples rowed in the dark, but the boat was still being battered by the waves in the middle of the lake.

In the fourth watch, while the sky was still black, someone was walking toward them across the water. The disciples screamed that it was a ghost, and then a familiar voice reached them. "Take heart. It is I." Peter shouted back: Lord, if it is you, tell me to come to you on the water. "Come."

Peter stepped out of the boat and walked a few steps on the water. But when he saw the fierce wind, fear swept over him and he began to sink. Lord, save me. At once Jesus reached out his hand and caught him. When the two of them climbed into the boat, the wind died down, and the disciples fell down before him.

words.text: Take courage. It is I. There is nothing to fear.
Come.
You of little faith, why did you doubt?
You really are the Son of God.

e32.note: In the Roman division of the night, the fourth watch ran from about three to six in the morning. John writes that the disciples saw Jesus after they had rowed twenty-five or thirty stadia, roughly five or six kilometers.
e32.reflect: When the fierce wind steals my gaze, whose hand do I look to again?

quiz.q: Why did Peter begin to sink while walking on the water?
options: He saw the wind and was afraid
He looked back at the boat
quiz.explain: When Peter saw the wind, he was afraid and began to sink (Mt 14:30).

e32.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Walks on the Sea, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e33.title: I Am the Bread of Life
e33.subtitle: A deeper food for those who came looking for a full stomach
story: The next day, the crowd that had eaten the bread crossed by boat to Capernaum looking for Jesus. He saw straight into their hearts. You are looking for me not because you saw signs, but because you ate the bread and were filled. Do not work for food that spoils and is gone, but for food that lasts forever.

The people brought up the manna their ancestors ate in the wilderness. Jesus answered that he himself was the true bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. A murmur spread through the synagogue at Capernaum. Isn't this the son of Joseph? How can he tell us to eat his flesh?

Saying this teaching was too hard, many of his disciples left and no longer walked with him. Jesus turned to the Twelve who remained. Do you want to leave too? After a moment of silence, Peter spoke. You have the words of eternal life, Lord. To whom would we go?

words.text: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty again.
Do not toil for food that soon disappears. Work for the food that endures to eternal life.
Do you want to go away as well?
Lord, you have the words of eternal life. Who else could we go to?

e33.note: The white limestone synagogue that stands in Capernaum today is thought to date from the fourth century or later, but the black basalt foundation beneath it may be a trace of the synagogue of Jesus' day.
e33.reflect: Do I ask the Lord only for bread, or do I seek him, the one who is life itself?

quiz.q: Where did Jesus teach about the bread of life?
options: In the Temple courts in Jerusalem
In a boat on the shore of the Sea of Galilee
quiz.explain: Jesus said these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (Jn 6:59).

e33.credit: James Tissot, You Follow Me for the Miracles, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e34.title: A Mother from the Region of Tyre
e34.subtitle: A faith content with crumbs
story: Jesus left Galilee and went north to the region of Tyre, a Gentile land by the sea. He entered a house and wanted no one to know he was there, but he could not stay hidden. A mother whose daughter was tormented by an evil spirit heard the news, came, and fell at his feet. She was not an Israelite.

Son of David, have mercy on me. She kept crying out, and the disciples, annoyed, urged him to send her away. Jesus' answer sounded cold. It is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs of the house. But the mother would not back down.

Yes, Lord. Yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table. Jesus' face brightened. Your faith is great. When she went home, she found the child lying peacefully on the bed, and the spirit that had tormented her was already gone.

words.text: Woman, your faith is truly great. Let it be done for you just as you wish.
Let the children be fed first. It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the house dogs.
Because you have answered this way, go home now. The evil spirit has already left your daughter.
Yes, Lord. But even the dogs under the table eat the crumbs the children drop, do they not?

e34.note: Tyre was a Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, Gentile territory in Jewish eyes. The word Jesus used refers not to wild dogs but to small dogs kept in the house.
e34.reflect: Even before a silence that feels like refusal, can I keep holding on to the Lord to the end?

quiz.q: How does the Gospel of Mark describe this woman?
options: A Greek, born in Syrian Phoenicia
The wife of a Roman centurion
The wife of a Galilean fisherman
quiz.explain: Mark describes her as a Greek woman, Syrophoenician by birth (Mk 7:26), while Matthew calls her a Canaanite woman (Mt 15:22).

e34.credit: James Tissot, The Canaanite's Daughter, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e35.title: Ephphatha — Be Opened
e35.subtitle: The day closed ears and a bound tongue were set free
story: Jesus left Tyre, passed through Sidon, and took the long way around to the Sea of Galilee, toward the region of the Decapolis. People brought him a man who was deaf and could barely speak, and begged him to lay his hand on him. Jesus took him aside, away from the crowd, to a quiet place.

Jesus put his fingers into the man's ears, spat, and touched his tongue. Then he looked up to heaven, sighed deeply, and spoke a single word. Ephphatha. Be opened. At once the blocked ears were opened and the tangled tongue was loosed, and the man began to speak clearly.

Jesus urged them to tell no one, but the more he told them, the farther the news spread. When he went up on a mountain, people brought him the lame, the blind, and those who could not speak, and seeing them healed, the crowd gave glory to the God of Israel.

words.text: Ephphatha. Be opened!
Everything he does is wonderful. He makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.

e35.note: Ephphatha is Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea in Jesus' time, and Mark often preserves such Aramaic expressions as they were spoken. The Decapolis was a region of ten Greek-style cities scattered east and south of the Sea of Galilee.
e35.reflect: What ears are closed and what words are bound within me, and where would the Lord say, be opened?

quiz.q: What does the word Ephphatha, spoken by Jesus, mean?
quiz.explain: Mark explains that Ephphatha means 'Be opened' (Mk 7:34).

e35.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Heals the Blind and Lame on the Mountain, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e36.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
e36.subtitle: A question asked beneath the rock where the spring bursts out
story: At the foot of Mount Hermon lies Caesarea Philippi, where the waters of the Jordan spring up from beneath the rock. In this unfamiliar land, lined with niches for foreign gods, Jesus asked his disciples as they walked along the road: Who do people say that I am?

Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah or Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Then who do you say that I am? Peter answered: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus called him blessed and gave him once again the name that means rock.

From then on, Jesus began to tell them that he must suffer many things in Jerusalem, be killed, and rise again on the third day. When Peter took hold of him and said this could never happen, Jesus rebuked him sharply. And he told all who wished to follow him to take up their own cross.

words.text: But you, what about you? Who do you say that I am?
Whoever wants to follow me must let go of self, take up their cross, and come after me.
What good is it to gain the whole world and lose your own life?
You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

e36.note: Philip the tetrarch named the city in honor of the emperor; today it is Banias. The cave and temple ruins once devoted to the god Pan still remain, and one of the main sources of the Jordan River springs up here.
e36.reflect: Not what others say, but who do I confess Jesus to be right now?

quiz.q: Which person was not among the answers the disciples reported when asked who people said Jesus was?
quiz.explain: The disciples reported that people called Jesus John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Mt 16:14). Moses is not mentioned.

e36.credit: James Tissot, Get Thee Behind Me Satan, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e37.title: Transfigured on the Mountain
e37.subtitle: Glory glimpsed for a moment on the mountain
story: Six days later, Jesus took only Peter, James, and John and went up a high mountain. As he prayed, his face shone like the sun and his clothes became dazzling white. When the drowsy disciples opened their eyes, Moses and Elijah were talking with Jesus.

They were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. Flustered, Peter blurted out: Lord, it is good for us to be here. Let me build three shelters. At that moment a bright cloud covered them, and a voice rang out from the cloud. This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.

The disciples fell face down and trembled. Someone laid a hand on their shoulders. Get up, do not be afraid. When they looked up, they saw only Jesus. Coming down the mountain, Jesus told them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

words.text: Get up. Do not be afraid.
Tell no one what you have seen until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.
Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but treated him however they pleased.
This is my Son, whom I love, my delight. Listen to him.

e37.note: The Gospels say only 'a high mountain.' Tradition has long identified it as Mount Tabor, but many scholars point to Mount Hermon, which is near Caesarea Philippi from the previous scene and much higher.
e37.reflect: When the dazzling moment passes and only Jesus remains, will I still listen to him?

quiz.q: Which two men appeared and talked with the transfigured Jesus?
quiz.explain: Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Jesus (Mt 17:3; Mk 9:4; Lk 9:30).

e37.credit: James Tissot, The Transfiguration, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e38.title: Who Is the Greatest?
e38.subtitle: He sets a child in the middle of them
story: On the way back to Capernaum, the disciples lagged behind, arguing in low voices. When they entered the house, Jesus asked: What were you arguing about on the road? No one answered. Who was the greatest, that had been their quarrel.

Jesus sat down, called the Twelve, took a little child, and stood the child in the middle of them. Then he took the child in his arms. Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all. Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.

Jesus told of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go looking for the one lost sheep. Peter asked: If my brother wrongs me, how many times must I forgive him? Is seven times enough? Jesus told him to forgive even seventy-seven times, and told the parable of a servant who was forgiven a huge debt yet would not forgive a small one.

words.text: Whoever wants to be first must stand behind everyone else and become the servant of all.
Unless you turn around and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
Not just seven times. Forgive even seventy-seven times.

e38.note: In the parable, the servant was forgiven ten thousand talents, while his fellow servant owed him a hundred denarii. One talent was about six thousand days' wages for a laborer, an almost unimaginable contrast.
e38.reflect: Do I forgive others while remembering how much I have been forgiven?

quiz.q: When Peter asked how many times he must forgive, what did Jesus answer?
quiz.explain: Jesus answered not seven times but seventy-seven times (Mt 18:22). The original can also be rendered 'seventy times seven,' and it means to forgive without end.

e38.credit: James Tissot, Jesus and the Little Child, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e39.title: Those Who Put Down Their Stones
e39.subtitle: The feast where he cried out for living water, and the words he wrote in the dust
story: It was the autumn Feast of Tabernacles, and Jerusalem was full of pilgrims and booths woven from branches. At a time when even his brothers did not believe in him, Jesus went up in secret, and halfway through the feast he began teaching in the Temple. On the last and greatest day of the feast, he stood and cried out: Anyone who is thirsty, come to me and drink.

The Temple guards sent to arrest him came back empty-handed and said: No one has ever spoken like this man. Early the next morning, the scribes and Pharisees dragged in a woman caught in adultery and made her stand in the middle. Moses told us to stone such a woman. What do you say?

Jesus bent down and wrote something on the ground with his finger. When they kept pressing him, he straightened up and said: Let the one among you who is without sin throw the first stone. One by one they slipped away, the oldest first, until only Jesus and the woman were left. Neither do I condemn you. Go.

words.text: If there is anyone among you who has no sin, let that person be the first to throw a stone at her.
Neither do I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.
Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. From the one who believes in me, living water will flow like a river.

e39.note: The story of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53 to 8:11, is missing from the earliest manuscripts. But it is regarded as an ancient tradition and appears in most Bibles, often set off with brackets or a note.
e39.reflect: Can I put down the stone in my hand and offer words of a new beginning instead of condemnation?

quiz.q: What did Jesus do when he bent down before the woman's accusers?
options: He looked up to heaven and prayed
He wrote on the ground with his finger
quiz.explain: Jesus bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger, and after he spoke, he bent down and wrote again (Jn 8:6, 8).

e39.credit: James Tissot, The Adulterous Woman--Christ Writing upon the Ground, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e40.title: Eyes Opened at Siloam
e40.subtitle: Eyes opened with mud and pool water
story: Passing through the streets of Jerusalem, Jesus saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked: Whose sin made this man blind, his own or his parents'? Jesus said it was neither. It happened so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

Jesus spat on the ground, made mud, spread it on the man's eyes, and told him to go and wash in the Pool of Siloam. Groping his way, the man went down the steps and washed his face in the water. And he came back seeing light for the first time in his life. That day was the Sabbath.

The Pharisees questioned him again and again, and even his parents, afraid, held their tongues. He held firm to the end. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see. After he was driven out of the synagogue, Jesus came looking for him, and he fell down, saying, Lord, I believe.

words.text: It was not his sin, nor his parents'. This happened so that the work of God might be shown through him.
While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam.
One thing I know for certain. I could not see, and now I can.

e40.note: In 2004, during sewer work in the south of Jerusalem, a stepped pool from the Second Temple period was discovered, and it is thought to be the Pool of Siloam in John's Gospel. Siloam means 'sent.'
e40.reflect: Even if I cannot explain it all, can I speak boldly of one thing the Lord has done for me?

quiz.q: According to John's Gospel, what does the name Siloam mean?
quiz.explain: John explains that Siloam means 'sent' (Jn 9:7).

e40.credit: James Tissot, The Blind Man Washes in the Pool of Siloam, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e41.title: The Good Samaritan and Two Sisters
e41.subtitle: One who becomes a neighbor, one who sits at his feet
story: An expert in the law stood up to test Jesus. What must I do to inherit eternal life? When the man himself recited the law to love God and neighbor, Jesus told him to do this and he would live. He asked again: And who is my neighbor?

Jesus told of the rugged road that goes down from Jerusalem to Jericho. A man was attacked by robbers and left half dead, and a priest and a Levite both passed by on the other side. But a Samaritan traveling that way saw him, was moved with compassion, and went to him. He poured oil and wine on his wounds, bandaged them, brought him to an inn, and cared for him.

As Jesus traveled on, he stopped at Martha's house in a certain village. Martha was busy with all the serving, while her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet listening to his words. When Martha poured out her frustration, Jesus gently called her name twice. Only one thing is truly needed.

words.text: Which of these three do you think became a neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?
Go and do the same.
Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about so many things. But only one thing is needed.
Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken from her.

e41.note: From Jerusalem to Jericho was about twenty-seven kilometers, a wilderness descent of more than a thousand meters. Luke says only 'a certain village,' but John's Gospel identifies the village of Martha and Mary as Bethany.
e41.reflect: Am I someone who debates who my neighbor is, or someone who becomes a neighbor first?

quiz.q: What money did the Samaritan give the innkeeper?
quiz.explain: The next day the Samaritan gave two denarii to the innkeeper and asked him to look after the man (Lk 10:35).

e41.credit: James Tissot, The Good Samaritan, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e42.title: I Am the Good Shepherd
e42.subtitle: The shepherd who calls his sheep by name
story: The shepherd comes in through the gate and calls his own sheep one by one by name, and the sheep know his voice and follow him out. Jesus borrowed this familiar scene to speak of himself. I am the gate for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

A few months later, in winter, it was the Feast of Dedication. As Jesus was walking in Solomon's Porch in the Temple, people gathered around him. How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. Jesus answered: My sheep hear my voice, and no one can snatch them out of my hand.

The Father and I are one. At these words they picked up stones again. Jesus slipped out of their grasp and withdrew across the Jordan, to the place where John had first baptized, and stayed there. And there many believed in him.

words.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.
I came so that the sheep may have life, and have it in overflowing abundance.
My sheep recognize my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
The Father and I are one.

e42.note: The Feast of Dedication is a winter festival commemorating how Judas Maccabeus, in 164 BC, recovered the Temple defiled by the foreign king Antiochus the Fourth and dedicated it again. Today it is Hanukkah.
e42.reflect: Among so many voices, do I recognize the voice of the shepherd who calls me?

quiz.q: Where in the Temple was Jesus walking during the Feast of Dedication?
quiz.explain: It was winter, the Feast of Dedication, and Jesus was walking in Solomon's Porch in the Temple (Jn 10:22–23).

e42.credit: James Tissot, The Good Shepherd, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e43.title: The Joy of Finding the Lost
e43.subtitle: A sheep, a coin, and a son
story: When tax collectors and sinners gathered around Jesus to hear him, the Pharisees and scribes muttered: This man welcomes sinners and even eats with them. So Jesus told them three stories about finding what was lost.

A shepherd who loses one of his hundred sheep leaves the ninety-nine and searches until he finds that one. A woman who loses one of her ten silver coins lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house looking for it. And once they find it, both call their neighbors to come and rejoice with them.

The younger son took his inheritance early, squandered it all in a far country, and longed to fill his stomach even with pig feed. Then he came home. While he was still a long way off, his father recognized him, ran to him, and embraced him. The father threw a feast, and when the elder son angrily refused to come in, the father went out himself to plead with him.

words.text: There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who comes back than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
This son of mine was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found. So let us celebrate together.
My child, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.
